title: The Funnel Math Sheet: How Many Cold Emails You Need for One Signed Client
description: Real cold email funnels from our campaigns, benchmarks to start with, a step-by-step calculator, spreadsheet formulas and the levers that lower your cost per client.
lead: This is the full funnel math sheet from the reel. It shows our real numbers from emails sent to signed contracts, gives you safe starting benchmarks, and walks you through working out how many emails your business needs every month, with formulas you can paste into a spreadsheet.
insider: This sheet comes from our campaign for a construction software company. The reply rate was below the 2026 average, and we still booked **31 qualified demos and 6 annual contracts**, because we aimed at real decision makers. Getting those numbers right for your business is the first thing we plan with every client.

blocks.text: The 4 numbers that run your funnel

items: **Interested rate:** interested replies ÷ all replies. Many replies are "no thanks" or out-of-office.

blocks.text: Multiply them together and you know how many emails one client costs. Change any one of them and the whole number moves.
Here are three of our real campaigns. They're very different businesses, which is exactly why you need your own numbers.

Look at the construction software campaign: its reply rate was **below the average**, and it still produced 6 annual contracts, because the emails went to real decision makers. A high reply rate from the wrong people is worth nothing.
Use these for your first plan, then **replace every guess with your own numbers after 2 to 4 weeks** of sending.

items: **Pick your goal:** how many new clients you want per month.
**Calls needed** = clients ÷ close rate. (2 clients ÷ 0.2 = 10 calls)
**Emails needed** = replies ÷ reply rate. (267 ÷ 0.03 = about 8,900 a month)
**Per working day** = monthly emails ÷ 22. (about 405 a day, so 14 inboxes, see our MATH guide)

blocks.label: Check the money
blocks.text: Multiply clients by your average deal value. If 2 clients bring $6,000 and the setup costs a few hundred dollars a month, the math works. If your deal is $200, cold email needs a much better conversion rate to pay off.
Put your numbers in cells B1 to B5 of a Google Sheet, then paste these formulas below them.
Every number multiplies the others, so improving any one of them by 2x halves the emails you need. But some are much easier to move than others.

blocks.text: Example: raise the reply rate in the plan above from 3% to 4.5% and you need about **5,900 emails a month instead of 8,900**. That's 5 fewer inboxes to buy and warm up.

blocks.label: Funnel prompt
blocks.text:
My goal: [number] new clients per month.
Average deal value: $[amount].
My numbers (use these guesses if I don't know): reply rate [3%], interested rate [15% of replies], call rate [25% of interested], close rate [20% of calls].

Calculate, step by step:
1) calls, interested replies, replies and emails needed per month,
2) emails per working day (22 days) and inboxes needed at 30 emails per inbox per day,
3) revenue if I hit the goal,
4) what happens to emails needed if I improve each rate by 50%, one at a time.
Tell me which rate to test first. Show everything in tables.

blocks.label: The real scoreboard
blocks.text: Reply rate is not the scoreboard. Booked calls and signed contracts are. 100 replies from the wrong people = $0.

faq.q: Why did the construction software campaign need so many emails per client?
faq.a: It sold annual software contracts to construction companies, a careful buyer with a long sales cycle. Simpler offers with faster decisions usually need fewer emails per client.

faq.q: How long before my own numbers are reliable?
faq.a: Give it at least 2 to 4 weeks and a few thousand emails before you trust the rates. Small numbers jump around a lot.
Better targeting. Emailing the right decision makers raises replies, interested replies and calls at the same time, more than any copy trick.
Count them as replies if your tool does, but never as interested. That's why the interested rate matters more than the reply rate.
